conclusion.justification: The report concludes that strong randomized-trial evidence demonstrates corticosteroids like dexamethasone increase survival and lower 28-day all-cause mortality among critically ill COVID-19 patients receiving respiratory support.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
**Conclusion: No—corticosteroids do not *ensure* survival, but strong randomized-trial evidence shows they increase survival among patients with severe or critical COVID-19 who need oxygen or mechanical ventilation.**

The pivotal RECOVERY randomized trial compared dexamethasone (6 mg daily for up to 10 days) with usual care in hospitalized patients. It reduced 28-day mortality in those receiving invasive mechanical ventilation: **29.3% with dexamethasone versus 41.4% with usual care**—an absolute reduction of about 12 deaths per 100 treated patients. Benefit also occurred in patients receiving oxygen without invasive ventilation. It did **not** improve mortality in people not needing respiratory support.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2021436

The result is not dependent on one trial. A prospective WHO REACT meta-analysis pooled **seven randomized trials** (1,703 critically ill patients across 12 countries) testing dexamethasone, hydrocortisone, or methylprednisolone. Compared with usual care/placebo, systemic corticosteroids were associated with lower 28-day all-cause mortality.  
https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2770279

Accordingly, WHO made a **strong recommendation** for systemic corticosteroids in severe and critical COVID-19, based on moderate-certainty evidence, while advising against them for non-severe disease.  
https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/479c227b-0999-4f4f-8cd6-838c0172bfc9/content

Thus, the accurate answer is: **yes, these drugs improve the odds of survival in critically ill COVID-19 patients—but they are not a guarantee and should be targeted to patients with severe/critical, oxygen-requiring disease under clinical supervision.**
